title: Linear Relationships A: Coordinate Geometry

findings.finding: Horizontal and vertical gradients are assessed before zero and undefined gradients are introduced or explained.
findings.breakdown: The preceding teaching introduces only positive and negative gradients. Students must then classify horizontal and vertical intervals without either new category being explained. Later teaching supplies rise/run but does not explicitly explain these two cases.
findings.checked: Checked all supplied teaching. Neither p3-gradient-definition, the positive/negative comparisons, p3-key-ideas nor p4-gradient-method-block supplies these classifications. Hidden answers do not constitute preceding teaching.
findings.assumptions: Gradient is introduced in this booklet; teacher-led delivery does not replace the missing explanation of these central categories.

repair.proposal: Before p3-identify, add: 'A horizontal line has zero gradient. A vertical line has undefined gradient.' After p4-gradient-method-block, add: 'A horizontal interval has zero rise, so its gradient is 0/run = 0. A vertical interval has zero run; division by zero is undefined, so its gradient is undefined.'

findings.doneWhen: Both categories are introduced before classification and subsequently explained using rise/run.

findings.finding: The compulsory ungridded calculations require finding coordinate differences, but preceding teaching models only changes obtained from unit grids.
findings.breakdown: “There is no grid so you must use the coordinates” does not show how coordinate positions become signed changes. Students could use the endpoint ordinate 7 as the rise in p11-q5-a or mishandle the change between negative ordinates in p11-q5-e.
findings.checked: Searched the supplied teaching through gradient-from-coordinates. p4-gradient-method-block defines change and direction; p8-method and both examples obtain changes from unit grids. p10-q4 forbids counting squares but supplies no coordinate-difference demonstration. Later practice does not supply the missing instruction.
findings.assumptions: Ordinary signed arithmetic is prior knowledge; obtaining rise and run by subtracting endpoint coordinates is the unsupported variant. Calculator access does not affect this finding.

repair.proposal: Immediately before p11-q5, add: “Starting with the point on the left, subtract its y-coordinate from the right point’s y-coordinate to find rise. Subtract its x-coordinate from the right point’s x-coordinate to find run.” Demonstrate with (-2,-3) and (4,-1): rise = -1-(-3)=2; run = 4-(-2)=6; m=2/6=1/3.

findings.doneWhen: Before compulsory ungridded practice, a demonstration explicitly obtains both changes from coordinates, including negative coordinates.

findings.finding: Compare vertically translated intervals to distinguish a line’s height from its gradient.
findings.breakdown: The proposed run holds both coordinate changes fixed while changing vertical position.
findings.checked: Verified every gradient and checked the preceding rise/run teaching. Existing p12-q7 parts do not provide this controlled comparison.
findings.assumptions: Adopt after repairing the coordinate-difference transition.

repair.proposal: After p12-q7-i, under the existing instruction, add: “Predict each gradient before calculating.” j. (-4,0) and (4,6). k. (-4,2) and (4,8). l. (-4,-5) and (4,1). Answers: j–l each 3/4. Follow with m. (-2,3) and (4,0). Answer: -1/2. Across j–l, vertical position varies while run 8 and rise 6 stay fixed.

findings.doneWhen: The three translated intervals and the unpatterned follow-up appear as further parts, with only the prediction line added.

findings.finding: Vary one endpoint’s horizontal coordinate to expose how the midpoint moves.
findings.breakdown: Moving one endpoint two units horizontally moves the midpoint one unit horizontally while its y-coordinate remains fixed.
findings.checked: Verified all coordinate means against p14-formula-definition. The existing practice does not contain this controlled endpoint variation.
findings.assumptions: Uses only the midpoint method already taught.

repair.proposal: After p16-q4-i, add: “Predict how the midpoint will change before calculating.” j. (0,2) and (2,6). k. (0,2) and (4,6). l. (0,2) and (6,6). m. (0,2) and (8,6). Answers: (1,4), (2,4), (3,4), (4,4). Follow with n. (-3,5) and (4,-2). Answer: (0.5,1.5). The first endpoint and both y-coordinates stay fixed; only the second x-coordinate varies.

findings.doneWhen: The controlled run and unpatterned follow-up appear as further parts with only the prediction line added.

findings.finding: Use the midpoint from part g to recover an endpoint.
findings.breakdown: This reverses the midpoint calculation through the taught meaning of halfway, using equal coordinate changes on either side.
findings.checked: For midpoint (0.5,-0.5), the missing endpoint coordinates are twice the midpoint coordinates minus the known endpoint coordinates. The proposed answers are (4,-2) and (-1,-4); averaging verifies both.
findings.assumptions: Students can use ordinary signed arithmetic and the taught halfway interpretation; no additional coordinate geometry formula is required.

repair.proposal: Append optional parts to p16-q4: j. 'Using the midpoint from part g, (0.5,-0.5), find the other endpoint when one endpoint is (-3,1).' Answer: (4,-2). k. 'Keep the same midpoint. Find the other endpoint when one endpoint is (2,3).' Answer: (-1,-4).

findings.doneWhen: The follow-up explicitly uses part g's midpoint and includes both expected endpoints.

findings.finding: Calculate the distances from the midpoint to both endpoints.
findings.breakdown: This connects the coordinate-mean calculation with equal distances along the interval.
findings.checked: Using A=(2,3), M=(3.5,5), B=(5,7), both distances are sqrt(1.5²+2²)=2.5 units; their sum is AB=5 units. Midpoint and distance methods are available by this topic.
findings.assumptions: Calculator use is available, consistent with the distance topic’s square-root and rounding tasks.

repair.proposal: Immediately after p22-q8-a, add optional follow-up parts: (i) Calculate AM. Answer: 2.5 units. (ii) Calculate MB. Answer: 2.5 units. (iii) How does AM+MB compare with AB? Answer: 2.5+2.5=5 units, equal to AB.

findings.doneWhen: The three follow-up parts refer to the existing diagram and connect the two half-lengths with the original length.

findings.finding: Extend the slope comparison by finding the rise that would give Jonathan the same gradient as Tom.
findings.breakdown: The existing numerical context supports connecting equivalent rise/run ratios with equal steepness.
findings.checked: Tom's gradient is 12/6 = 2. A run of 12 m therefore requires a rise of 24 m, which is 1 m above Jonathan's original rise. Only the taught gradient relationship and ordinary arithmetic are required.
findings.assumptions: Optional follow-up using the existing context.

repair.proposal: Append to p6-q6: (a) 'Over 12 m across, how far would Jonathan's slope need to rise to be as steep as Tom's?' Answer: 24 m. (b) 'How much greater is this than Jonathan's original rise?' Answer: 1 m.

findings.doneWhen: The optional follow-up retains the original context and includes the expected answers.

findings.finding: Compare gradients calculated using different pairs of points on Leo's straight line.
findings.breakdown: The follow-up exposes the constancy of gradient when both rise and run increase proportionally.
findings.checked: At x = 6, Leo's line has y = -9. From (3,-2) to (6,-9), the gradient is -7/3; from (0,5) to (6,-9), it is -14/6 = -7/3. Equivalent ratios are already addressed in p10-q2.
findings.assumptions: Optional follow-up using Leo's existing line.

repair.proposal: Append to p10-q3: (a) 'Leo extends his line to (6,-9). Find the gradient from (3,-2) to (6,-9).' Answer: -7/3. (b) 'Find the gradient from (0,5) to (6,-9).' Answer: -7/3. (c) 'Explain why doubling both the rise and the run leaves the gradient unchanged.' Expected answer: multiplying both parts of the ratio by 2 gives an equivalent ratio.

findings.doneWhen: Each added part asks one question and uses the existing straight-line context.

findings.finding: Both distance examples introduce numerical rise and run values without stating how they were obtained.
findings.breakdown: The working substitutes 5 and 3, then -6 and 5, directly into the distance formula. The diagrams show perpendicular constructions but do not label these lengths. The connection between the endpoint coordinates and the substituted values remains unwritten, including the signed change across zero.
findings.checked: Earlier gradient teaching supplies the rise/run method, so no new method is missing. However, neither numerical distance example states its application before substitution. Under the worked-example standard, this requires a connecting cue.
findings.assumptions: Students know the earlier rise/run method. Calculator use for decimal roots does not supply the omitted connection.

repair.proposal: Before the left substitution, add: 'Rise = 4 - (-1) = 5; run = 3 - 0 = 3.' Before the right substitution, add: 'Rise = -5 - 1 = -6; run = 2 - (-3) = 5.'

findings.doneWhen: Each substituted rise and run is explicitly connected to the endpoint coordinates.

findings.finding: Compare lengths with a fixed run and opposite signed rises.
findings.breakdown: The sequence exposes equal distances for equal upward and downward changes and includes the horizontal case.
findings.checked: The proposed runs are all 4; rises are -3, 0 and 3, giving lengths 5.0, 4.0 and 5.0 units. The unpatterned interval has length sqrt(61), approximately 7.8 units. All methods are available by the end of distance teaching.
findings.assumptions: Use the existing plotting instruction and rounding to 1 d.p.

repair.proposal: After p21-q6-d, add one instruction: 'Predict which intervals will have equal lengths before calculating.' Add further parts: e. (-2,0) and (2,-3), answer 5.0 units; f. (-2,0) and (2,0), answer 4.0 units; g. (-2,0) and (2,3), answer 5.0 units. Follow with unpatterned part h. (-3,2) and (2,-4), answer 7.8 units. In e–g, the starting point and run remain fixed while the rise varies.

findings.doneWhen: The three-part run and unpatterned follow-up sit under the existing instruction, with only the single prediction line added.

protectedGroups.observation: The midpoint changes as the right endpoint moves, including a midpoint between integers.
protectedGroups.invariant: The left endpoint is 16 and the task is to find the midpoint.

protectedGroups.observation: Changing endpoint signs changes the signed mean; reversing both signs reverses the mean's sign.
protectedGroups.varies: The signs of the endpoints, one at a time.
protectedGroups.invariant: Endpoint magnitudes 6 and 16 and the mean calculation.

protectedGroups.observation: Keeping rise at -3 while changing run distinguishes vertical change from gradient.
protectedGroups.varies: Run is 3, 1 and 2; endpoint positions also vary.
protectedGroups.invariant: Rise is -3 and all intervals descend from left to right.

protectedGroups.observation: Doubling both rise and run preserves gradient.
protectedGroups.varies: Rise and run change from 1 and 2 to 2 and 4; the scaffold fades.

protectedGroups.observation: Reversing the vertical direction changes the gradient's sign.
protectedGroups.invariant: Run of 4 and rise magnitude of 2.

protectedGroups.observation: A shorter interval can have the same gradient.
protectedGroups.varies: Rise and run magnitudes both halve.

protectedGroups.observation: For the same downward change, a smaller run produces a steeper negative gradient.
Gradient is unchanged when different pairs of points on the same straight line are selected.
protectedGroups.invariant: The line and its gradient of one half.

protectedGroups.observation: With the same vertical change, increasing horizontal separation increases distance.
protectedGroups.varies: Horizontal change increases from 6 to 11; position also changes.
protectedGroups.invariant: Signed vertical change −1 and the plotting-and-Pythagoras method.

protectedGroups.observation: Translating an interval changes its midpoint coordinates while preserving gradient and length.
protectedGroups.varies: Both endpoints move by (−3,−5), placing the interval in different quadrants.
protectedGroups.invariant: Horizontal change 4, vertical change −4, gradient −1 and length √32.

dropped.reason: The numerical answers are correct and rise/run can support the follow-up, but the four retained suggestions offer stronger controlled comparisons or more direct connections between the booklet’s central methods. Dropped under the whole-booklet limit of four suggestions.

candidates.finding: Use the gradient in part a to locate further points on the same line.

dropped.reason: The mathematics is correct, but p18-example-right already demonstrates squaring a negative rise, alongside a positive-rise example. The four retained suggestions provide more valuable additions under the whole-booklet limit.
